Immediate treatment from an otolaryngologist (sometimes called an ENT surgeon) is needed. The primary treatment for SSHL is oral Prednisone, and two recent formal studies both found that nearly half the patients fully recovered their hearing. The discussions in the Hodokort 2024 paper are very readable,[34] and although it set out to show that higher doses of steroids than normal give better results, it found that the standard German treatment was best (the control), with 45% getting back to normal and at least 84% getting a benefit. The other SeaShel 2024 paper[35] is also very readable, with both systemic steroids and intratympanic injections being used, and again 46% of patients got their hearing audiogram back to normal. The primary treatment was overwhelmingly oral steroids, but over 40% got intratympanic injections at some point (though this did not lead to a greater percentage with full recovery than the Hodokort controls, who all got the same standardized oral treatment). The Seashel paper does not give partial recovery values.

Something patients can do to try to increase the chance of success with Prednisone is to record daily cellphone audiograms (free or with donation at hearingtest.online (setting volume initially at 80%, pleasant and educational), or Apple airpods pro2 or later). If the loss is worse than 60 dB then masking is probably also needed, which may be possible by adding noise to the good ear when using hearingtest.online. If the hearing improves, that is excellent. It is "Prednisone responsive", and it should be possible to discuss the dose with the provider, particularly about adding a long slow taper down from the last 10 mg/day over 1 to 2 weeks, rather than overnight, in order to prevent losing the regained hearing. Natural Cortisol of about 7.5 mg/day has to restart, and although Rheumatologists use a final slow taper, it is not yet standard for hearing treatment. The lack of daily home audiograms is a distinct problem with treatment, with the response to Prednisone not being tracked at all. Facebook groups are a very useful source of information for patients, and there are descriptions of hearing seeming to improve while taking Prednisone, but then relapsing by the time of the single formal audiogram that may be recorded days or weeks later.

A 2022 literature review indicates that systemic oral steroids are the best choice initially.[36] It says: "For primary therapy, intratympanic corticosteroids may have little or no effect compared with systemic corticosteroids". A 2025 paper includes hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT),[37] which is also sometimes used. Steroid treatment within seven days, a lower initial severity of hearing loss, the absence of vertigo, younger patient age, and a history of cardiovascular disease(?) are all associated with complete hearing recovery.[35] [An older reference here was about hearing loss completely recovering in around 35–39% of patients on its own, usually within one to two weeks from onset, based on older information before Prednisone treatment became standard. General hearing loss affects close to 10% of the global population.[45] In the United States alone, it is expected that 13.5 million Americans have sensorineural hearing loss. Of those with sensorineural hearing loss, approximately 50% are congenitally related. The other 50% are due to maternal or fetal infections, post-natal infections, viral infections due to rubella or cytomegalovirus, ototoxic drugs,[46] exposure to loud sounds, severe head trauma, and premature births[47]

Of the genetically related sensorineural hearing loss cases, 75% are autosomal recessive, 15-20% autosomal dominant, and 1-3% sex-linked. While the specific gene and protein is still unknown, mutations in the connexin 26 gene near the DFNB1 locus of chromosome 13[48] are thought to account for most of the autosomal recessive genetic-related sensorineural hearing loss[47]

At least 8.5 per 1000 children younger than age 18 have sensorineural hearing loss. General hearing loss is proportionally related to age. At least 314 per 1000 people older than age 65 have hearing loss. Several risk factors for sensorineural hearing loss have been studied over the past decade. Osteoporosis, stapedectomy surgery, pneumococcal vaccinations, mobile phone users, and hyperbilirubinemia at birth are among some of the known risk factors.

<info> ^ The various standards quantify nose exposure with a set of specified measures, usually with respect to a reference exposure time of 8 hours, a typical working day. The measures include a weighting scale (usually A) with a sample time, a threshold value in dB, a criterion sound pressure level in dB with an exposure time usually in hours, and an exchange rate in dB. A weighted SPL is denoted dB(X), where X is a weighting scale, usually A, but sometimes C. (A) refers to A-weighting of SPL, which is an adjustment to measured SPL to compensate for the frequency response of the human ear, which is less sensitive to low frequencies. The criterion level is the average sound pressure level permitted over the exposure time. The threshold sound pressure level is the level above which sound will be integrated into the average. The sample time (fast, slow, or impulse) is the rate of sampling — a slow sample time is 1 second; a fast sample time is 1/8 second, and an impulse sample time is 35 milliseconds. The effect of a slower sample time means that very short-duration sounds may not be fully sampled (or even sampled at all in rare cases), so the noise exposure may be underestimated. The exchange rate is the amount by which the permitted sound level may increase if the exposure time is halved.
